title: Question and Response Dynamics in Public Service Encounters
abstract: Provides more than 200 verbatim transcripts of authentic German conversations between street-level bureaucrats and citizens together with annotations of all question-response pairs. The study distinguishes response behavior including direct and more evasive responses in an authentic institutional setting.

admission.reason: The institutional corpus and annotated question-response pairs are relevant vocabulary, but the abstract only distinguishes response behavior such as direct versus evasive responses. It does not show multi-question alignment, exact proposition/span targeting, partial answers, unanswered subquestions, or multi-link structure. The capability therefore does not materially close the current gaps, and the identifier is UNCHECKED.

title: Characterizing the Response Space of Questions: a Corpus Study for English and Polish
abstract: Develops a fine-grained taxonomy intended to cover the full response space of questions rather than only direct answers. The taxonomy is grounded in corpus studies of English dialogue corpora and compared with Polish conversational data.

admission.reason: This is highly relevant to F3, but the supplied abstract describes the earlier corpus taxonomy that the 2022 'Characterizing the Response Space of Questions: data and theory' candidate explicitly extends with broader corpus coverage, annotation reliability, and formalization. With limited reading slots, the later extension materially dominates this candidate for the present gaps. Both identities are UNCHECKED, so this rejection assumes the supplied relationship is accurate.

title: UgChDial: A Uyghur Chat-based Dialogue Corpus for Response Space Classification
abstract: Introduces two-party and multi-party chat data containing explicitly identified question-response pairs. The pairs are annotated using a fine-grained response-space taxonomy, providing chat-based empirical evidence about different ways a question can be responded to.

admission.reason: The chat corpus and explicit question-response pairs are relevant, but the abstract mainly applies a fine-grained response-space taxonomy. It does not show multi-question turns, unanswered-subquestion detection, exact proposition targets, or a workplace domain. The response-taxonomy contribution substantially overlaps the stronger 2022 response-space candidate, so it does not justify another reading slot. Identity is UNCHECKED.

title: A Distance-Aware Multi-Task Framework for Conversational Discourse Parsing
abstract: Constructs utterance dependency structures for multi-party conversations while combining graph-based and transition-based parsing. The framework is specifically designed to improve both short- and long-distance discourse links, which is relevant when a response targets a non-adjacent antecedent.

admission.reason: The method improves short- and long-distance discourse links, but the abstract does not show capabilities central to the open gaps: exact proposition/span targets, partial response scope, question-resolution status, multiple antecedents, no-link outcomes, or workplace communication. It is generic discourse-parsing transfer evidence and is weaker for this round than the admitted QUD and domain-specific link candidates. Identity is UNCHECKED.

title: A corpus-based taxonomy of question responses
abstract: Uses corpus evidence to develop a taxonomy of responses to questions rather than treating all following turns as equivalent answers. The taxonomy is intended to support formal and computational models of dialogue response behavior.

admission.reason: The corpus-based response taxonomy is directly relevant in principle, but the supplied contribution is substantially subsumed by the later 2022 response-space paper, which additionally reports annotation reliability and a formalized account across several corpora and languages. Reading both is unlikely to materially strengthen the current streams unless the later paper explicitly depends on unresolved details from this precursor. Identity is UNCHECKED.

title: Structured Dialogue Discourse Parsing
abstract: Treats dialogue discourse parsing as finding discourse links and corresponding relations throughout multi-participant conversations. The method jointly optimizes structural links and relations and performs structured decoding rather than independently assigning local pairwise labels.

admission.reason: The abstract establishes generic structured dialogue-link and relation prediction, but it does not indicate partial answers, target-span scope, multiple simultaneous antecedents, explicit no-link handling, or workplace communication. The capability is therefore broadly relevant to F2/F9 but does not materially strengthen a current open gap beyond stronger admitted candidates. Identity is UNCHECKED.

title: Improving Dialogue Discourse Parsing via Reply-to Structures of Addressee Recognition
abstract: Models dialogue discourse structure by establishing discourse links and exploits addressee-recognition reply-to structures as a related source of structural supervision. A task-aware framework learns the shared and distinct structure of reply-to and discourse links on STAC and Molweni.

admission.reason: The paper studies the relationship between addressee reply-to structures and dialogue discourse links, but the abstract does not show proposition-level response scope, question resolution, acceptance/rejection targets, multiple links, or no-link outcomes. It is useful generic discourse-parsing transfer work, but the present reading round needs more direct evidence. Identity is UNCHECKED.

title: An Annotation Scheme of A Large-scale Multi-party Dialogues Dataset for Discourse Parsing and Machine Comprehension
abstract: Proposes an annotation scheme for large-scale multi-party Ubuntu chats containing explicit discourse structure together with question-answer information. The representation supplies discourse links among conversational units rather than only message-level reply structure.

admission.reason: The verified Ubuntu-chat dataset supplies explicit discourse structure and question-answer information, but the supplied abstract does not establish the specific capabilities still missing: multi-question alignment, partial or unanswered subquestions, exact target spans, or multi-antecedent response scope. It is a valuable general discourse resource, but admitting it here would consume a slot without clearly closing a current gap.

title: Dialogue Discourse Parsing as Generation: A Sequence-to-Sequence LLM-based Approach
abstract: Recasts dialogue discourse parsing as a text-to-text generation task so that a sequence-to-sequence language model generates discourse structures directly. The approach is evaluated on STAC and Molweni, where the target representation contains dialogue discourse links and relations.

admission.reason: Recasting generic dialogue discourse parsing as generation changes the modeling approach, but the abstract does not show a new capability for the project's central problems of partial response scope, exact proposition targeting, no-link outcomes, multi-question resolution, or workplace evidence. It therefore does not materially strengthen this round's streams. Identity is UNCHECKED.

title: Opening Up Closings
abstract: Provides a foundational conversation-analytic study of how conversational sequences are organized and brought to closure. Its analysis of sequential organization helped establish the interactional framework from which adjacency-pair and conditional-relevance accounts of responses developed.

admission.reason: This is foundational conversation-analysis work on sequential organization and closings, but the supplied abstract does not provide the specific capabilities required here: proposition-level antecedent resolution, reply-scope annotation, multi-question answer alignment, acceptance target identification, or composite antecedents. Its historical importance is not sufficient reason to spend a reading slot in this targeted round. Identity is UNCHECKED.

title: Contributing to discourse
abstract: Argues that discourse contributions require interlocutors to establish mutual belief that an utterance has been understood sufficiently for current purposes. It develops conversational contribution units and a collaborative account of how material enters common ground.

admission.reason: The collaborative common-ground account and conversational contribution units are conceptually relevant to grounding, but the supplied abstract does not show exact antecedent targeting, partial acceptance/rejection scope, question-response alignment, multiple antecedents, or an evaluation scheme for unresolved links. The contribution is too foundational and broad for the specific open gaps in this round. Identity is UNCHECKED.
